about: The people's own things go on speaking against the wooden people. The dogs say they were chased off and never fed, and that now they will bite and eat their masters; the grindstones say they were ground every day, holi, holi, huqui, huqui, and now will grind their owners' flesh; the griddles and pots say they were blackened and burned, and now will burn them in turn; and the hearthstones turn on them too. The wooden people run in despair: they climb onto the houses and the houses fall in, they climb the trees and the trees shake them off, they try to get into the caves and the caves close before their faces. So they were ruined, and the monkeys of the forest are said to be what is left of them, a sign of the people who were only effigies carved of wood. Then, while there is only a faint light on the face of the earth and no sun or moon yet, one being makes himself great: Vucub Caquix, Seven Macaw. He boasts that the bone of his face is silver and glitters with jewels, that his teeth shine blue-green, that his nose gleams like the moon and his seat is silver, and that he is the sun and the moon for the people; but he is not the sun, and his sight does not reach far. The part ends by announcing how he died.

sentences.t: “Cax xiban chique; xoh itio; ix chi cut xquix cati chic,” xꜭha ri qui ꜩi, cac chiquech.
sentences.l: “Pain you-did to-us; you-bit-us; you now then we-shall-bite(?)-you in-turn,” said the their dogs, cac(?) to-them.
sentences.i: “You did us harm; you bit us; now it is your turn: we shall bite you,” their dogs said to them.
sentences.n: The household things answer their owners one by one, and the dogs begin. cax 'pain, harm' (modern k'ax); xiban 'you did': x- + i- 'you (pl.)' + ban 'do'. Inside the speech chique is taken as 'to us' (chi + qe), not 'to them': Ximénez's qu stands for both k and q, and the dogs mean themselves; the toggle shows chiqe. xoh itio 'you bit us': x- + oh 'us' + i- 'you (pl.)' + tio 'bite' (ti + -o, as xtio in the last part); ti is 'eat flesh' as well as 'bite', and if cac below names the fowls, 'you ate us' would be theirs. In ix chi cut, chi is taken as chic 'in turn' with its c shared with cut, as in the earlier parts. xquix cati chic is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has xquixcah, a dot and chic, and the looped letter is read t (Brasseur x-qu'yx qati chic). It is taken as xqu- (xchi- 'shall' before a vowel) + ix 'you' + ca- 'we' + ti 'bite', 'we shall bite you', like xquix catio at the end of the dogs' speech below. cac chiquech is uncertain: both letters are plain c, Brasseur's OCR is garbled here, and his French ('their dogs and their hens') takes cac as ac 'fowl', as he read qui aq 'their turkeys' where the manuscript has qui caa in the list at the end of the last part. The word is left out of i, and the toggle respells its letters; chiquech 'to them'.

sentences.t: Are cu ri ꜫaa: “Xoh coconic ivumal; hutaꜫih, hutaꜫih, xꜫec, zaquiric, amaꜫel, holi, holi, huqui, huqui ca vach ivumal;
sentences.l: This then the grindstones: “We-were-tormented(?) by-you; every-day, every-day, it-darkened, it-dawned, always, holi, holi, huqui, huqui our face by-you;
sentences.i: Then the grindstones: “We were tormented by you; every day, every day, at dusk and at dawn, always holi, holi, huqui, huqui went our faces because of you;
sentences.n: ꜫaa 'grindstone', the metate on which maize is ground (modern ka'). Here Ximénez writes it with the 3-shaped tresillo, where the last part had caa with a c. The word is certain (Brasseur caa, and his note 'caa in Quiché'), so the toggle shows kaa, as in the last part, not a respelled q'aa. xoh coconic 'we were tormented': x- + oh 'we' with a verb in -ic. coconic is not otherwise known (Brasseur qokonic), and 'tormented' follows his French. ivumal 'by you (pl.)': i- + umal, the umal of rumal 'by, because of'. hutaꜫih 'every day' (hun 'one' + tac 'each' + ꜫih 'day'), doubled. xꜫec 'it grew dark' (from ꜫeꜫ 'black') and zaquiric 'it dawned' (zac 'white'): dusk and dawn, a couplet. amaꜫel 'always'. holi, holi, huqui, huqui is the sound of the hand-stone on the grinding stone (Brasseur: the noise the stone makes when maize is ground on it). ca vach 'our faces', the grinding surfaces.

sentences.t: are ta nabe ca patan chivach, ix ta na vinac.
sentences.l: this then first our service before-you, you then still(?) people.
sentences.i: this was the service we gave you first, when you were people still.
sentences.n: patan 'service, duty, tribute', what is owed to a lord. chivach 'before you': chi + iv- 'your (pl.)' + vach 'face', a relational noun like chuvach. ix ta na vinac is uncertain: ix 'you (pl.)', ta and na particles, vinac 'people'. It is taken as 'when you were still people'; Brasseur reads it as 'now that you have ceased to be people', which the words do not plainly say.

sentences.t: Vacamic cut xchitih ca chucab; xchicaqueech, xchicahoc puch itiohil,” xꜭha ri qui ꜫaa chique.
sentences.l: Now then you-shall-try our strength; we-shall-grind(?), we-shall-crush(?) also your-flesh,” said the their grindstones to-them.
sentences.i: Now you shall feel our strength: we shall grind, we shall crush your flesh,” their grindstones said to them.
sentences.n: vacamic 'now'. xchitih 'you shall try, you shall taste': xchi- 'shall' + i- 'you (pl.)', run into the chi, + tih 'try', the verb of tihtobeh in the second part; what you try here is what you feel. ca chucab 'our strength' (Brasseur chugab, that is ꜫ; Ximénez writes plain c, and the toggle shows chuq'ab', as the second part's chuꜫab 'arm'). xchicaqueech and xchicahoc are xchi- 'shall' + ca- 'we' + a verb: queech 'grind' and hoc 'crush, pound', both taken from Brasseur's French ('we shall grind and reduce your flesh to powder'); the senses are inferred. The manuscript has a clear double e and a final ch in queech; Brasseur prints queeh. itiohil 'your flesh', i- 'your (pl.)'. Out in the narrator's frame chique is 'to them' again. ri qui ꜫaa is the tresillo spelling of the grindstones again; the toggle shows kaa.

sentences.t: Are cu ri qui ꜩi xꜭha chic, ta xꜭhauic: “Naquipa rumal mavi chiya ca va?
sentences.l: This then the their dogs said again, when it-spoke: “What for not you-give our food?
sentences.i: Then their dogs spoke in their turn, and said: “Why did you not give us our food?
sentences.n: xꜭha chic 'said in turn', then ta xꜭhauic 'when it spoke': the dogs are spoken of as one, with singular verbs. Naquipa rumal 'why': naqui 'what' + pa + rumal 'because of' (Brasseur, word for word, 'what-for'). chiya 'that you give': chi + i- 'you (pl.)' + ya 'give'. ca va 'our food': this va is food, the maize tortilla (modern wa), not va 'this'.

sentences.t: Xa coh mucunic, xa pu coh icuxih vloc, coh izac pu vloc; yacal vbi ca cheel ivumal, ta quix vaic.
sentences.l: Only we looked-on(?), only also us you-chased(?) hither, us you-drove(?) also hither; raised(?) its-name(?) our stick by-you, when you-were-eating.
sentences.i: We had only to look on, and you would chase us off, you would drive us out; your stick was kept raised for us while you ate.
sentences.n: coh 'we, us (ongoing)', c- + oh, as in the earlier parts: the dogs tell what used to happen. mucunic is taken as 'looking on' (Brasseur 'scarcely were we looked at'); the sense is inferred. coh icuxih 'you chased us', coh izac 'you drove us', both with i- 'you (pl.)' and vloc 'hither', out from the hearth; both senses follow Brasseur's French and are inferred. In izac the letter is a z, not the tz ligature (Brasseur tzak); it is printed as seen. yacal 'raised, held up' (yac 'lift'). vbi 'its name' does not fit plainly here (perhaps 'what is called our stick'), and it is left out of i. ca cheel 'our stick', from che 'wood'. ta quix vaic 'while you ate': quix 'you all (ongoing)' + va 'eat' + -ic.

sentences.t: Xere coh ivuchaah vi; mavi coh ꜭhauic.
sentences.l: Thus us you-treated(?) there; not we spoke.
sentences.i: That is how you treated us; we could not speak.
sentences.n: xere 'just so, this is how'. ivuchaah is not otherwise known: i- 'you (pl.)' + a verb, and 'treated' follows Brasseur's French ('that is how you treated us'); the toggle respells the letters. mavi coh ꜭhauic 'we did not speak': the dogs' old silence, set against their speech now; speech is what the animals were refused in the second part.

sentences.t: Ma ta cu mi xoh camic chive?
sentences.l: Not then then just-now we-died to-you?
sentences.i: Did we not die because of you?
sentences.n: xoh camic 'we died': x- + oh 'we' + cam 'die' + -ic. chive 'to you, by you (pl.)': chi + ive. mi 'just now', as in mixix in the second part. The question is hard. Read as it stands it is 'did we not just now die by you?'; Brasseur takes it as 'otherwise we would not now kill you'. The sense is uncertain.

sentences.t: Hupacha mavi mi xix nauic, xix nau ta cut chivih ta cut?
sentences.l: How not just-now you-thought, you-thought then then about-yourselves then then?
sentences.i: How is it that you did not think, that you did not think of yourselves?
sentences.n: Hupacha 'how', as in the second part. xix 'you (pl.) did': x- + ix. xix nauic and xix nau 'you thought': nau 'think', the verb of naoh 'mind', first with -ic and no object, then with chivih 'about yourselves' (chi + iv- 'your' + ih 'back': to think behind oneself is to take thought). The negative of the first half carries into the second. Not thinking is the wooden people's fault, the charge of the last part.

sentences.t: Xoh zach vi; vacamic cut xchitih ca bac ꜭo pa ca chi; xquix catio,” xeꜭha ri ꜩi chique, ta xcut qui vach.
sentences.l: We-were-lost(?) there; now then you-shall-try our bone(s) there-are in our mouth; we-shall-eat-you,” they-said the dogs to-them, when were-struck(?) their face.
sentences.i: We were brought to nothing; now you shall feel the bones that are in our mouths: we shall eat you,” the dogs said to them, and their faces were struck.
sentences.n: xoh zach 'we were lost, brought to nothing' (zach 'lose, be lost'); Brasseur's French ('it is we who destroy you') takes it otherwise, and the sense is uncertain. xchitih as in the grindstones' speech. ca bac ꜭo pa ca chi 'our bones that are in our mouth', the teeth: bac 'bone', chi 'mouth' (the same letters as chi 'at, in'; the toggle shows chi'). xquix catio 'we shall eat you': xqu- 'shall' (xchi- before a vowel) + ix 'you' + ca- 'we' + tio 'bite, eat', the verb of xoh itio above. xeꜭha 'they said' is plural now. ta xcut qui vach 'their faces were struck', as in the last part; the sense of xcut is uncertain.

sentences.t: Are chi cu ri qui xot, qui boh xꜭhau chic chique: “Cax, ra xiban chique; xac ca chi, xac ca vach;
sentences.l: This in-turn then the their griddles, their pots spoke again to-them: “Pain, ra(?) you-did to-us; blackened(?) our mouth, blackened(?) our face;
sentences.i: Then their griddles and their pots spoke to them in their turn: “You did us pain and harm: our mouths were blackened, our faces were blackened;
sentences.n: chi before cu is again taken as chic 'in turn', with its c shared. xot 'griddle', the clay comal; boh 'pot'. As in the dogs' speech, chique is 'to them' in the frame and 'to us' (chiqe) inside the speech. ra is not otherwise known; next to cax 'pain' it is taken as a second word for harm (Brasseur 'evil and damage'), which is inferred. xac ca chi, xac ca vach 'our mouths, our faces', a couplet: xac is taken as 'blackened with soot' from Brasseur's French ('smoking our mouths and our faces'), and the sense is inferred.

sentences.t: amaꜫel oh ꜩacal chuvi cac, coh icato; mavi cax xca nao.
sentences.l: always we set(?) on-top-of fire, us you-burned(?); not pain we-felt.
sentences.i: always we were set on the fire, and you burned us; and we felt no pain.
sentences.n: oh ꜩacal 'we (were) set': ꜩacal is taken as 'placed, set' (Brasseur 'exposing us to the fire'), which is inferred. chuvi cac 'on top of the fire': cac is ꜫaꜫ 'fire' (as in the next sentence), here with plain c twice (Brasseur gag); the toggle shows q'aq'. coh icato 'you burned us' is a doubtful reading: the letter after ca is the ß-ligature, which elsewhere stands for ti or tz; t is printed, with Brasseur's qato, and 'burn' follows him. mavi cax xca nao 'we did not feel pain': xca- 'we (did it)' + nao, nau 'know, feel' with the transitive -o. Brasseur takes it as a complaint, 'though we felt nothing'; the pots may mean that they bore it without a word.

sentences.t: Xchitih cut, xquix caporoh,” xcha ri qui boh; ronohel xcute qui vach.
sentences.l: You-shall-try(-it) then, we-shall-burn-you,” said the their pots; all struck(?) their face.
sentences.i: Now you shall feel it: we shall burn you,” said their pots; and all of them struck at their faces.
sentences.n: xchitih again 'you shall try (it)', and xquix caporoh 'we shall burn you', built like xquix catio: poroh 'burn'. xcha 'said', the verb of xecha in the first part, written here beside xꜭha. ronohel xcute qui vach as at the end of the last part: all of them struck at their faces. xcute is taken as the verb of xcut, and its sense is uncertain.

sentences.t: Are ri abah ri qui xcub chi ta ninic chi pe pa ꜫaꜫ taꜫal chi qui holom; cax xban chique.
sentences.l: This the stone the their hearthstones, that then rushing(?) that come from fire set(?) at their head; pain was-done to-them.
sentences.i: And the stones, their hearthstones, came rushing out of the fire straight at their heads; harm was done to them.
sentences.n: xcub 'hearthstone', one of the three stones that hold the griddle over the fire (Brasseur qixcub; Ximénez writes plain c, and the toggle shows xk'ub', the modern word). The rest of the sentence is hard. chi ta ninic chi pe pa ꜫaꜫ is taken as 'that they rushed, that they came out of the fire'; ninic is not otherwise known. taꜫal chi qui holom is taken as 'set at their heads' (taꜫal perhaps 'set up, standing'). Brasseur reads it the other way round, the fire blazing up under the people's heads laid on the hearth. Both readings are uncertain. In pa ꜫaꜫ 'in the fire' the 3-shaped tresillo stands twice (Brasseur gag), and once in taꜫal. cax xban chique 'harm was done to them', the cax of the speeches now in the narrator's voice.

sentences.t: Anilabic que mal, malihab chic;
sentences.l: Running(?) they mal(?), malihab(?) now;
sentences.i: They ran in haste, pushing one another, in despair;
sentences.n: anilabic is taken as 'running, in haste'. que 'they (ongoing)': c- + e 'they'. mal and malihab are not otherwise known; 'pushing one another' and 'in despair' follow Brasseur's French ('running, pushing one another, full of despair') and are guesses. malihab is a doubtful reading: the l and h are retraced in heavy ink, and the letters could also be taken as mahlab (Brasseur malihab).

sentences.t: que rah acanic chuvi ha, xa chi vvlih ha que ꜩac vloc; que rah acan chuvi che, que ꜭhaquix vloc ruma che; que rah oc pa hul, xa chi yuch hul chi qui vach.
sentences.l: they-want climbing on-top-of house, only then fell-in(?) house, they-fell hither; they-want climb on-top-of tree, they-are-shaken-off(?) hither by tree; they-want enter in hollow, only then closed(?) hollow at their face.
sentences.i: they tried to climb onto the houses, but the houses fell in and they fell down; they tried to climb up into the trees, and the trees shook them off; they tried to get into the caves, and the caves closed before their faces.
sentences.n: Three tries and three failures, in three parallel lines. que rah 'they want, they tried': que is c- + e 'they'; rah is r- 'his, its' + ah 'want', the form of xrah in the second part, which seems to stand here as a fixed word 'want to' after a plural subject (Brasseur 'ils voulaient'). The wanted act follows it (acanic, acan 'climb', oc 'enter'). Here ha is 'house' (modern ja), not ha 'water' (ja'): Brasseur reads 'houses', and the toggle shows ja. vvlih 'fell in, collapsed' is inferred (Brasseur 'the houses, falling down, made them fall'). que ꜩac vloc 'they fell down': ꜩac 'fall'. que ꜭhaquix 'they were shaken off': the image has gh, that is ꜭh, where Brasseur prints chakix; the sense is his. ruma is rumal 'by' without its l. hul 'hollow, pit', here the caves; yuch 'close' is inferred. In the third line the manuscript's que looks like quo (quorah); it is printed que, as in the two lines before.

sentences.t: Quehe cut vcayohic vinac ꜯac, vinac bit, e ꜩixel, e ꜩalaꜩoxel chi vinac;
sentences.l: Thus then its-ruin(?) person built, person shaped, they to-be-overthrown(?), they to-be-overturned(?) as person;
sentences.i: Such was the ruin of the people built, the people shaped, people to be overthrown, people to be overturned;
sentences.n: vcayohic 'its ruin' (Brasseur gayohic, that is ꜫ; Ximénez writes plain c); the sense is his and inferred. vinac ꜯac, vinac bit 'a person built, a person shaped', the couplet of the creators' plan, now in their ruin. ꜩixel and ꜩalaꜩoxel are taken as nouns of what is to be done to someone, 'ones to be overthrown, to be overturned' (Brasseur 'people destined to be destroyed and overturned'); ꜩalaꜩ is a doubled root, and both words are uncertain. e marks them plural; chi vinac 'as people'.

sentences.t: xmayxic, xcutuxic qui chi, qui vach conohel.
sentences.l: were-ruined(?), were-destroyed(?) their mouth, their face all.
sentences.i: ruined were their mouths, destroyed were their faces, every one of them.
sentences.n: xmayxic, xcutuxic are the verbs of qui mayxic, qui cutuxic 'their ruin, their destruction' at the start of the flood in the last part, now with x- 'was': passives in -x. As there, the senses follow Brasseur and are inferred; Ximénez writes plain c in xcutuxic where Brasseur has q. qui chi, qui vach 'their mouths, their faces' (chi 'mouth'). conohel 'all of them': qui- 'their' made c- before a vowel + onohel, as ronohel is r- + onohel.

sentences.t: Xꜭha cut, are vetal ri ꜭoy ꜭo pa quechelah vacamic;
sentences.l: It-is-said then, this its-sign the monkey there-is in forest now;
sentences.i: And it is said that the monkeys that live in the forests now are their sign;
sentences.n: Xꜭha 'it is said': the story points outside itself, to the present. vetal 'its sign, its trace': v- 'its' + etal 'sign, mark' (modern retal; Brasseur prints r'etal, but the manuscript clearly has vetal here and twice below). The toggle respells the letters, v before a vowel as w, as ve 'teeth' below; Brasseur notes that etal also means 'descendants'. ꜭoy 'monkey', a small kind (Brasseur: a very small monkey found in the highlands of the Verapaz). ꜭo 'there is, they are'. quechelah 'forest', the spelling used since the second part. vacamic 'now, today'.

sentences.t: are xꜭohe vi vetal, rumal xa che qui tiohil xcohic rumal Ahꜯac, Ahbit.
sentences.l: this remained there its-sign, because only wood their flesh was-put(?) by He-who-builds, He-who-shapes.
sentences.i: that is the sign that was left of them, because their flesh was only wood, set there by the Builder and the Shaper.
sentences.n: xꜭohe vi 'it remained there, it came to be'. xa che qui tiohil 'only wood (was) their flesh', as the last part told of the man's tz'ite' and the woman's reed pith. xcohic 'was put, was set', from coh 'put' with -ic, is inferred (Brasseur 'was composed'). Ahꜯac, Ahbit 'He who builds, He who shapes', the creators' second pair of titles, rendered in i as the Builder and the Shaper.

sentences.t: Are cu ri ꜭoy queheri vinac chi vachinic, vetal hule vinac ꜯac, vinac bit, xa poy, xa pu aham che.
sentences.l: This then the monkey like person in its-showing-a-face, its-sign hule(?) person built, person shaped, only effigy, only also carved wood.
sentences.i: And so the monkey looks like a person: it is the sign of the people built, the people shaped, who were only effigies, only things carved of wood.
sentences.n: queheri 'like, as': quehe 'thus' + ri. chi vachinic 'in its appearing, in its look': vachin 'show a face, bear fruit', from vach 'face'. hule is not otherwise known; Brasseur takes the line as 'a sign that it is of another generation of human beings', and the word is left out of i. xa poy, xa pu aham che 'only effigies, only carved wood': the house phrase poy, aham che, split by xa ... xa pu 'only ... and only'. The story of the wooden people ends here, with the monkeys of the forest as what is left of them.

sentences.t: Are cut xa hubic zacnatanoh vvach vleu; mahabi ꜫih.
sentences.l: This then only a-little bright(?) its-face earth; not-yet sun.
sentences.i: Now there was only a little light on the face of the earth; there was no sun yet.
sentences.n: A large capital A in the manuscript begins a new episode here (Brasseur's chapter four). hubic 'a little', the modern jub'iq', which the toggle shows. zacnatanoh is taken as 'it was faintly bright', from zac 'white, light'; the rest of the word is not clear, and the sense is Brasseur's ('little clarity'). mahabi 'there is not, not yet'. ꜫih is both 'day' and 'sun': the sun has not yet risen, and the first dawn is still to come.

sentences.t: Hun cut cu nimarizah rib, Vvcub Caquix vbi.
sentences.l: One then he-makes-great himself, Seven Macaw his-name.
sentences.i: But there was one who made himself great, Vucub Caquix by name.
sentences.n: cu nimarizah is taken as c- (ongoing) + v- 'he' + nimarizah 'make great' (nim 'great' + -ariza 'make'), with rib 'himself' (r- 'his' + ib 'self'): 'he makes himself great', he boasts. The c- and v- are written cu, the same letters as the particle cu 'then'; the toggle shows ku. Vvcub Caquix is vucub 'seven' + caquix 'macaw', the scarlet macaw: Seven Macaw (Brasseur Vukub-Cakix, 'Seven Macaws'). The name is kept in English. Ximénez writes Vvcub twice on this page and Vucub twice on the next; v and u are one letter in his hand, and both are printed as written.

sentences.t: Ꜭo nabe cah, vleu; xa ca moymot vvach ꜫih, ic.
sentences.l: There-was first sky, earth; only it-is dim(?) its-face sun, moon.
sentences.i: The sky and the earth were there already; only the face of the sun and the moon was dim.
sentences.n: Ꜭo 'there is, there was'. nabe 'first, already'. cah, vleu 'sky, earth', the pair of the first part. ca moymot 'is dim, veiled': ca- marks the ongoing state, and moymot is taken from Brasseur ('veiled'). ꜫih, ic 'sun, moon': ic (modern ik') is both 'moon' and 'month'. Neither has yet risen; what shines in their place is the macaw.

sentences.t: Ca ꜭha cu ri: “Xavi xere vzaquetal vinac ri xbutic; queheri naual vinac vꜭoheic.
sentences.l: Says then the(-one): “Just only-this its-white-sign(?) person the was-flooded; like spirit-power person its-being.
sentences.i: And he says: “This alone is the bright sign of the people who were flooded; their being is like that of people of spirit power.
sentences.n: Ca ꜭha 'he says': ca- marks the ongoing action, the story slipping into the present, as cacha in the second part. xavi 'just, also'; xere 'this is it, only this'. vzaquetal is taken as v- 'its' + zac 'white, bright' + etal 'sign' (Brasseur divides u zak etal); the sense is uncertain. ri xbutic 'the ones who were flooded': the manuscript has rÿ, an r and a y with a diaeresis (Brasseur riy). It is printed ri, the article, which is uncertain. naual 'spirit power'; vꜭoheic 'its being', as qui ꜭoheic in the second part. What Vucub Caquix means here is not clear, perhaps that the drowned people, for all their spirit power, have left nothing to rival him.

sentences.t: In nim quiꜭohe chic chuvi vinac ꜯac, vinac bit.
sentences.l: I great I-am now on-top-of person built, person shaped.
sentences.i: I am great; I stand now above the people built, the people shaped.
sentences.n: In 'I', the first-person pronoun, which runs through the macaw's speech. quiꜭohe 'I am, I exist': taken as c- (ongoing) + in 'I' + ꜭohe 'be', run together, with the n of in not written (compare qui poco vi ivib 'you shall multiply' in the second part, where the x of ix is not written, and quinel 'I come out' below, where the n is). As written, qui- could also be 'they'; the In before it decides for 'I'. Brasseur takes it as future, 'I shall be great once more'. chuvi 'on top of, over'. In this vinac ꜯac the final c is retraced as a heavy L-shape, a blot or a correction; the word itself is plain.

sentences.t: In vꜫih, in pu vzac, in nai pu riquil; ta chuxoc.
sentences.l: I its-sun, I also its-light, I likewise also its-moon; then let-it-be.
sentences.i: I am their sun, I am their light, and I am their moon. So be it.
sentences.n: vꜫih 'its sun', vzac 'its light, its whiteness', riquil 'its moon' (r- + ic 'moon' + -il): v- and r- are 'its', the people taken as one, and i has 'their'. in ... in pu ... in nai pu 'I ... and I ... and I likewise' builds a triplet. ta chuxoc 'so be it', the creators' word of assent (chuxoc 'let it be'), now in the boaster's mouth.

sentences.t: Nim nu zaquil; in binibal, in pu chacabal rumal vinac, rumal puvac vbac nu vach;
sentences.l: Great my light; I means-of-walking, I also means-of-standing(?) by person, because silver its-bone my face;
sentences.i: Great is my light: I am what people walk by, what people stand by, for the bone of my face is silver;
sentences.n: nu 'my'. zaquil 'light, clarity', as in the first part. binibal 'means of walking' and chacabal 'means of standing' are the pair of the deer's charge in the second part (cahcah ibinibal, ychacabal 'on all fours your walking, your standing'), now made the macaw's claim: by his light people go about; chacabal remains inferred. puvac 'silver, precious metal' (Brasseur: any precious metal, today said mostly of silver). vbac nu vach 'the bone of my face', that is the eyes, as vbac qui vach in the last part.

sentences.t: xa ca tiltotic chi yamanic raxa cuval; nay pu ve raxcavacoh chi abah, queheri vva cah.
sentences.l: only it-is glittering with jewels(?), green stones(?); likewise also teeth(?) shining-blue-green(?) with stone, like its-face sky.
sentences.i: they glitter with jewels, with green stones; and my teeth too shine blue-green with stone, like the face of the sky.
sentences.n: ca tiltotic 'it glitters': the manuscript looks like cahiltotic, with the looped letter read t, as elsewhere in this hand (Brasseur tiltotic). yamanic and raxa cuval are taken as precious stones, 'jewels, green stones' (Brasseur 'resplendent with precious stones'); raxa is 'green-blue'. In cuval Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has q (that is ꜭ); the toggle respells the letters as written. ve is taken as 'teeth', following Brasseur ('my teeth shine'), who writes v'e, that is v- 'its' + e, not ve 'if' of the earlier parts; this is uncertain. raxcavacoh 'shining blue-green' is not otherwise known; rax 'green-blue' stands at its head. vva cah 'the face of the sky': va for vach, as Brasseur notes.

sentences.t: Are cu ri nu ꜩam zachuluhuh chi nah queheri ic;
sentences.l: This then the my nose gleams(?) at far like moon;
sentences.i: And my nose gleams white from afar, like the moon;
sentences.n: ꜩam 'nose, tip': the macaw's great beak. zachuluhuh is taken as 'gleaming white', from zac 'white' (Brasseur zakhuluhuh, 'shine'); the rest of the word is not clear. chi nah 'from far off'. queheri ic 'like the moon'.

sentences.t: puvac cut nu calibal; ca zacpaque vvach vleu ta quinel vloc chuvach nu calibal.
sentences.l: silver then my seat(?); it-is brightening(?) its-face earth when I-come-out hither before my seat(?).
sentences.i: and my seat is silver; the face of the earth grows bright when I come out before my seat.
sentences.n: calibal is taken as 'seat, throne', a noun of place in -ibal (Brasseur galibal, that is ꜫ; Ximénez writes plain c both times); the sense is inferred, and the toggle respells the letters as written. ca zacpaque 'it grows white, grows bright' (zac 'white'), inferred. ta quinel vloc 'when I come out hither': c- (ongoing) + in 'I' + el 'go out'. In the manuscript ta quinel vloc is written as one word, divided here; Brasseur's OCR is garbled at this point.

sentences.t: Quehe cut in ꜫih vi, in pu ic, rumal zaquil al, zaquil ꜭahol.
sentences.l: Thus then I sun there, I also moon, because-of white child, white son.
sentences.i: So I am the sun, and I am the moon, for the clear light of the children, the clear light of the sons.
sentences.n: The boast comes to its point: he is the sun and the moon. zaquil al, zaquil ꜭahol 'the clear light of the child, the clear light of the son': al and ꜭahol, a mother's child and a father's son, are the pair in Alom, Ꜭaholom. Brasseur notes that the two together usually mean 'subjects, vassals': the macaw claims to be sun and moon for the people under him.

sentences.t: Ta chuxoc, rumal chi nah copon vi nu vach.”
sentences.l: Then let-it-be, because at far it-reaches there my face.
sentences.i: So be it, for my sight reaches far.”
sentences.n: copon 'it reaches, it gets there': c- (ongoing) + opon 'arrive (there)'. nu vach 'my face, my eyes', that is, my sight. The claim is denied at once in the next lines: his sight does not reach far at all.

sentences.t: Ꜭha ri Vvcub Caquix. Ma ca quiꜩih are ta ꜫih ri Vucub Caquix; xere cu nimarizah rib ri vxic, vpuvac.
sentences.l: Says the Seven Macaw. Not (ca) truly this then sun the Seven Macaw; only he-makes-great himself the his-vxic(?), his-silver.
sentences.i: So spoke Vucub Caquix. But Vucub Caquix was not truly the sun; he only made himself great with his finery and his silver.
sentences.n: Ꜭha 'says' closes the speech. Ma ca quiꜩih 'not, truly': the image reads maca, where Brasseur prints Ma-cu; ca is printed as the image shows, and its sense here is uncertain. quiꜩih 'truly, in truth' (ꜩih 'word'). cu nimarizah rib 'he makes himself great', as above. vxic is uncertain: Brasseur's French has 'his precious stones', and the word may be the xik' 'wing' of modern dictionaries, which would suit a macaw; 'finery' in i is a guess that covers both, and the toggle respells the letters. vpuvac 'his silver, his wealth'.

sentences.t: Xere cut tocol vi vvach ri chi cube vi; mana ronohel ta vxecah copon vi vvach.
sentences.l: Only then cut-off(?) there his-face the where settles(?) there; not all then under-sky it-reaches there his-face.
sentences.i: His sight was cut short where it came to rest; it did not reach the whole world under the sky.
sentences.n: tocol 'cut off, ended', inferred (Brasseur togol: 'his sight ended where it fell'); Ximénez writes plain c. chi cube vi 'where it settles': cube is taken from cub 'sit, settle', inferred. vxecah 'the world': xe 'under, at the foot of' + cah 'sky', all that is under the sky (Brasseur's note), with v- 'its'. mana ... ta 'not': ta follows what is denied. copon vi vvach 'his sight reaches', the boast of the speech, now denied.

sentences.t: Maha cut qui quiloc vvach ꜫih, ic, chumil; maha oc ca zaquir oc.
sentences.l: Not-yet then their seeing(?) its-face sun, moon, star; not-yet yet it-is dawning yet.
sentences.i: The face of the sun, the moon and the stars could not yet be seen; it had not yet dawned.
sentences.n: maha 'not yet' (compare mahabi), with oc 'yet' after it and again after the verb: maha oc ca zaquir oc 'not yet does it dawn'. qui quiloc is taken as 'their being seen', following Brasseur ('one did not yet see'); the form is not clear. chumil 'star' (modern ch'umil).

sentences.t: Quehe cut cu cobizah vi rib ri Vucub Caquix chi ꜫihil, chi iquil;
sentences.l: Thus then he-makes-proud(?) there himself the Seven Macaw in sun-ness, in moon-ness;
sentences.i: So Vucub Caquix puffed himself up as the sun, as the moon;
sentences.n: cu cobizah ... rib 'he makes himself proud' (Brasseur 'made himself superb'), with cu as in cu nimarizah: c- + v- 'he'. cobizah is inferred. chi ꜫihil, chi iquil 'in sunhood, in moonhood': ꜫih 'sun', ic 'moon', with -il, which makes an abstract noun, as zaquil from zac.

sentences.t: xa maha chi cutun oc, chi calahob oc vzaquil ꜫih, ic; xa xuraih nimal icouen.
sentences.l: only not-yet that appear yet, that become-clear yet its-light sun, moon; only he-desired greatness icouen(?).
sentences.i: for the light of the sun and the moon had not yet appeared, had not yet come clear; he only longed for greatness, to rise above all.
sentences.n: cutun 'appear', the root of vcutunizaxic in the preamble, and calahob 'become clear', the root of vcalahobizaxic beside it: the book's opening pair comes back to say that the light is not yet shown. Ximénez writes plain c in calahob; the toggle shows q'alajob', as in the preamble. xuraih 'he longed for': x- + v- 'he' + raih 'desire, long for' (Brasseur 'désirait'). It is taken as its own verb, not the ah 'want' of xrah, which would leave the r- unexplained after v-; the analysis is inferred. nimal 'greatness'. icouen is clear in the image but not otherwise known (Brasseur prints nimaliqouen and gives 'to surpass'). It may come from a verb of passing, but its meaning is uncertain, and 'to rise above all' in i is a guess.

sentences.t: Are ta xbanic butic cumal poy, aham che.
sentences.l: This then was-made flood by-them effigy, carved wood.
sentences.i: It was at this time that the flood was made, because of the effigies carved of wood.
sentences.n: Are ta 'it was then that'. xbanic butic 'the flood was made', as in the last part. cumal 'by them, because of them': the flood came on account of the wooden people. The macaw's boast is set in the age of the flood, before the sun had risen.

sentences.t: Quehe cut xchicabyih chic ta xcamic Vucub Caquix, ta xchacatahic, ta xbanatahic vinac rumal Ahꜯac, Ahbit.
sentences.l: Thus then we-shall-say again when died Seven Macaw, when he-was-overcome(?), when was-made person by He-who-builds, He-who-shapes.
sentences.i: And so we shall tell, in turn, how Vucub Caquix died, how he was brought low, and how people were made by the Builder and the Shaper.
sentences.n: The narrator speaks. xchicabyih 'we shall say, we shall tell': xchi- 'shall' + ca- 'we' + byih 'say', as in ca byih 'let us say' in the second part. Three clauses with ta 'when': xcamic 'he died' (cam 'die'); xchacatahic 'he was brought low', the verb used of the animals in the second part, with the sense inferred; and xbanatahic 'was made, came to be done', from banatah, as vbanatahic in the last line of the first part. The next part tells how two boys bring the macaw down.
